items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Octopuses change colour while being colour-blind
items.claim: Cephalopods produce sophisticated colour displays — mimicking corals, fish, sand — using chromatophore cells embedded in the skin. Their actual eyes have only one photoreceptor type. They cannot distinguish red from green.
items.prompt: How do octopuses match colour without seeing it?

options.text: They have hidden colour vision we haven't found
Their SKIN contains opsin proteins — the same light-sensitive receptors used in eyes — likely giving the surface itself wavelength-sensitivity that the eyes lack
Other octopuses signal the colour to them

items.reveal_title: Distributed colour vision via opsin-expressing skin
items.reveal:
Cephalopod skin expresses several genes (including r-opsin and rhodopsin-like proteins) usually found in eyes. Ramirez and Oakley (2015) showed Octopus bimaculoides skin responds to specific wavelengths.

The hypothesis: the chromatic information bypasses the brain entirely. The skin senses ambient colour and adjusts the chromatophore display locally without needing centralised colour vision.

It's also possible they exploit the chromatic aberration of their unusual U-shaped pupils to extract colour information from a single photoreceptor type — Stubbs and Stubbs (2016) — but the experimental support is mixed. Either way, cephalopod colour matching is a fascinating biological riddle.
items.why: Vision is assumed to happen in eyes and brains. In cephalopods it may happen distributed across the body.

items.title: Lizards aren't cold-blooded — they outsource thermoregulation
items.claim: Reptiles are usually called 'cold-blooded'. They aren't — many maintain body temperatures within 1-2 C of their preferred range. They do it behaviourally: basking on rocks, retreating to shade, postural adjustments — instead of metabolically.

options.text: Body temperature regulated primarily by external heat sources (sun, surfaces) rather than internal metabolic heat production; the animal's behaviour does the thermoregulation

items.reveal:
Endotherm vs ectotherm is about the SOURCE of body heat, not the temperature itself:
- Endotherm: internal heat from metabolism. Mammals and birds. Maintains body temperature by burning calories continuously.
- Ectotherm: external heat from environment. Reptiles, amphibians, fish, invertebrates. Maintains body temperature by movement and posture.

A desert lizard might bask flattened against a north-facing rock at dawn (warming up), move to shade at midday (cooling off), retreat into a burrow at night. Body temperature can be held within 1-2 C of an ideal value (~35-37 C for many lizards) — surprisingly mammal-like, achieved completely without metabolic heat.

Advantages of being ectotherm: much lower energy requirements. A reptile can survive on ~10% of the food a mammal of equivalent size needs. Snakes can fast for months.

Disadvantages: limited cold tolerance, dependent on environmental cues, slow at low temperatures. Reptiles cannot live in deep polar regions.

Many 'cold-blooded' fish, like tuna, are partially endothermic in muscle and brain (regional endothermy). And some plants (Symplocarpus, skunk cabbage) generate metabolic heat to melt snow and attract pollinators — endothermic plants exist.
items.why: 'Cold-blooded' is a misleading term. Reptiles regulate body temperature carefully — they just do it with behaviour and the sun, not with the calories you'd otherwise burn.
